comments.author: Alexander Terp
comments.body:
**The intended design, settled: a config file per daemon, written by
Muster when it starts one, and handed to that daemon alone.** Muster
owns `scrollback` (and whatever follows) in `~/.muster/config.toml`,
translates it, and the user never learns which daemon read what.

That is the same move already made for the renderer, so the half that is
ours needs no permission and is small: `~/.muster/state/libghostty.conf`
is written every launch from what the config file said, and a derived
herdr config beside it works the same way - derived, not editable, and
worth reading because it answers what Muster actually told the daemon.

**Confirmed there is no way to do it today**, checked rather than assumed
while settling this: v0.8.0 is the newest herdr tag, `config_dir()` reads
`XDG_CONFIG_HOME` or `HOME` and nothing else, `herdr server` has no
`--config`, and the only `HERDR_*` variables herdr reads anywhere are
debug, test and Windows-input ones. There is no path to hand a daemon a
config without handing its panes the same directory.

**One workaround was considered and rejected**, so nobody spends an
afternoon rediscovering it: point the daemon's `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` at a
Muster-private directory holding its own `herdr/` plus a symlink to every
other entry of the real `~/.config`. Reads and writes to directories that
already exist pass straight through, so it very nearly works. It fails on
*new* top-level entries - a program that creates `~/.config/something`
creates it inside Muster's private directory, where nothing else will
ever look for it. Muster could sweep strays back on the next launch, but
then Muster is repairing somebody's config directory, which is well
outside its business and an excellent way to lose their data. A pane runs
arbitrary programs; this is not a risk to take for a scrollback setting.

**A wrinkle to design for rather than discover: the config has to land
where the daemon can read it.** A window can be attached to a daemon on
another machine, so "write it on the fly" is trivial locally and a file
that has to reach the far side over the existing ssh master for a devenv.
Per-daemon is right for a second reason too - two machines can want
different answers, and a single Muster-wide daemon config would have to
pretend otherwise.

comments.author: Alexander Terp
comments.body:
**Unblocked, and the blocker's premise was wrong.** a_28adIUgPE says the
per-pane `env` map exists only on `layout.apply`. At the pinned 0.8.0 it
is on every pane-creating call: `PaneSplitParams.env`
(`src/api/schema/panes.rs:12`), and the same field routed through the same
`normalize_launch_env` by `tab.create` (`src/app/api/tabs.rs:73`) and
`workspace.create` (`src/app/api/workspaces.rs:51`). Checked against
`~/src/herdr` at `346411f`, tag v0.8.0, matching `deps/herdr.pin`.

**The mechanism.** The daemon gets `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` pointing at a
Muster-owned directory under `~/.muster/state/`, holding a
`herdr/config.toml` Muster writes. Every pane-creating call then passes
the user's own `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` back in `env`, so a pane's git, editor
and shell look where they always did. If the user never set one, pass the
empty string: the XDG spec treats unset and empty identically, so that is
a faithful restore rather than an approximation.

**This answers the objection in the comment on a_28adIUgPE**, which is
worth spelling out because it was the reason for preferring a flag. The
argument there was that a flag cannot leak while an environment variable
has to be scrubbed, and scrubbing is "a discipline the caller cannot
verify from outside". Per-pane env inverts that: the restore is a
parameter on each pane-creating intent rather than a process-wide state
somebody has to remember to undo. A conformance case can assert every
pane-creating intent carries it, so a new pane-creating path that forgets
fails the gate instead of leaking quietly.

**All three candidates are reachable, including the third.** Scrollback
depth and update checks become keys in Muster's own `config.toml`,
translated onward into the daemon's file exactly as `[font]` and
`[colors]` are translated into `libghostty.conf`. `default_shell` and
`shell_mode` are fixed too, though by a different route than the other
two: `pane.split` reads `self.state.default_shell` with no per-call
override (`src/app/api/panes.rs:57`), so what a pane runs still comes from
the daemon's config - which is now a file Muster writes rather than one
the user's own terminal setup wrote.

**Knock-on that makes this worth doing early.** Per-pane env is also how
Muster sets `MUSTER_PANE`, which is how `muster` inside a pane knows where
it is without reading a `HERDR_*` variable. That makes this card a
prerequisite for a_26BJb2n6o rather than a neighbour of it.

**Shape, as the description already sketched.** A derived
`~/.muster/state/herdr.toml` on the same terms as `libghostty.conf`:
rewritten every launch, not editable, and worth reading precisely because
it answers "what did Muster actually tell the daemon".

a_28adIUgPE stays open as an ergonomics ask rather than a blocker.

comments.author: Alexander Terp
comments.body:
**Landed, and by a different mechanism than this card settled - because the premise both
cards rested on is wrong.** `HERDR_CONFIG_PATH` exists at the pinned 0.8.0: `config_path()`
reads it (`src/config/io.rs:169`), `Config::load()` calls that, `run_server` calls
`Config::load()`. It is a plain `pub const` in `src/config.rs:38`, documented in `herdr
--help`, and present in the shipped binary's own strings. Verified against the binary rather
than the source: a scratch daemon started with it set read the file it named and ignored the
one in its `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`.

**It is a better lever than the private config directory, and the reason is what it does not
move.** herdr resolves its socket from `config_dir()` and its config file from `config_path()`,
which are independent - so this moves the file and leaves the socket, the session state and
the data directory exactly where they were. A private `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` would have moved all
four: `own_socket_path` and its five conformance cases would have changed, and the daemon
running when this shipped would have been orphaned with somebody's agents in it. It also
shrinks the failure mode of a forgotten restore from "this pane's git, nvim and gh look in
Muster's directory" to "this pane's `herdr` reads Muster's file".

**What shipped.** `scrollback_bytes` and `[shell]` (`command`, `mode`) in
`~/.muster/config.toml`; a derived `~/.muster/state/herdr.toml` written by the core just
before the daemon is started, on the same terms as `libghostty.conf`; `HERDR_CONFIG_PATH`
supplied to the daemon beside `LANG` and dropped from what is carried, so a stray export
decides nothing. Update checks are written off unconditionally and are not offered, which is
why the file is written even when nothing is configured. Every pane-creating call carries the
user's own config path back in `env`, and a conformance case reads herdr's recorded schema to
assert that every method herdr declares an `env` on is one Muster sends one on - so a fourth
pane-creating path fails the gate rather than leaking.

**Three facts found while building it, each of which changed something.** Neither new setting
is live: `scrollback_limit_bytes` and `default_shell` are both arguments herdr takes when it
builds a pane's terminal, so both reach panes opened afterwards and no others - one rule, and
the one `pane_padding` already has. `[update]` *is* live, which is what makes calling
`server.reload_config` worth doing at all: saving the config file rewrites the derived one and
asks the daemons Muster owns to read it again, because the daemon is started and never
stopped, so "relaunch to pick this up" would have been a lie. And a pane herdr restores after
a daemon restart carries no launch environment at all, so the restore covers panes Muster
makes and is a stated limit rather than a gap.

**One case this cannot reach, by construction.** A daemon started by a Muster from before this
change has no `HERDR_CONFIG_PATH` in its environment, and herdr publishes no method that would
let Muster ask. It resolves itself the first time that daemon is not running.

**Also fixed on the way past:** `tools/smoke-launch.py`'s cold-start scenario pinned its shell
in the herdr config the daemon no longer reads. It now pins it in the Muster config and
asserts the app named its own derived file at `daemon.starting` - so that tier proves the
mechanism end to end rather than passing by luck.

Remote daemons are out of scope and carded separately. `new_cwd` is now unreachable from
Muster's config; herdr's default is `follow`, which is what `intent.rs` already documents
Muster relying on, so nothing changed - worth a card only if somebody asks for it.

creator: Alexander Terp
description:
A person who wants deeper scrollback has to learn that herdr exists, find
its config file, and edit it. The desideratum now says that is wrong -
"where Muster acts on the answer, the way to ask is Muster's, never the
dependency's" - and this is the card that makes it true of the config
file rather than only of the README.

**Blocked on a_28adIUgPE**, and only on that.

**It is an inconsistency, not a boundary.** The config rule already
reads: a setting is Muster's when Muster acts on the answer, *including
the ones it only translates onward for libghostty*. Muster does not
consume `[font]` or `[colors]` either - it writes a derived
`libghostty.conf` and hands it over. Translating onward to the daemon is
the same move. It has simply never had a mechanism, and the absence of a
mechanism turned into a rule in the docs.

Three candidates, in increasing order of how much they matter:

1. **Scrollback depth.** The motivating case, and purely ergonomic: it is
   obviously a user setting, and today it is somewhere else.
2. **What a pane runs** (`default_shell`, `shell_mode`). Muster decides
   what a pane *is*; a `default_shell` somebody set for their own
   terminal silently deciding what every Muster pane runs is the surprise
   a_28adIUgPE already describes.
3. **Update checks.** `version_check` and `manifest_check` default to
   **true** in herdr, so Muster's bundled daemon - pinned by version and
   checksum, downloaded and verified by `./dev`, shipped inside the app -
   is checking for its own updates against a config file Muster does not
   own and cannot read the intent of. This one is not ergonomics. Pinning
   the daemon is what makes "green suite means it works" mean anything,
   and right now nothing stops the pinned daemon being told to move off
   the pin by a file Muster never sees.

The blocker, verified again against 0.8.0 while writing this: herdr
resolves its config directory from `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`, panes inherit the
daemon's environment, and so a private config directory for the daemon is
a private config directory for every pane's git, editor and shell.
`config_dir()` reads `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` or `HOME` and nothing else, and
`herdr server` has no `--config` flag.

**When it lands, the shape is already prototyped.** Muster writes
`~/.muster/state/libghostty.conf` every launch: derived, not editable,
and worth reading precisely because it answers "what did Muster actually
tell the renderer". A `herdr.toml` beside it, on the same terms, gives
the same answer for the daemon - and the first question when a pane opens
the wrong shell becomes a file you can read rather than a guess about
whose config won.

Two things to decide when writing it, rather than discover:

- **Which of the three are settings at all.** Update checks are not a
  user's choice in a bundled daemon - they are a thing Muster should turn
  off and not offer, the way it does not offer to change which herdr it
  runs. Scrollback plainly is a user's. What a pane runs is the arguable
  one, and it interacts with the harness-agnostic goal.
- **What happens to a user's existing herdr config.** Somebody who set
  `default_shell` for their own terminal will have it stop applying to
  Muster's panes, which is the point, and it is still a behaviour change
  worth naming in a release note rather than letting people find.
title: ⚙️ Settings a user should never leave Muster to change
